Being in circumstances that remind me of the event (eg, being in the dark).
Any form of physical contact with others

I feel ashamed of what happened to my body
I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened

issues.item: Fear of Rage: I will not be able to control my anger and will do something terrible
issues.explanation: The appraisal of feared uncontrollable rage is not well supported by the rest of the profile. There are no corresponding trigger, threat, memory, or strategy items suggesting anger-driven reactivity, aggression risk, or conflict; the other appraisals instead center on shame and hopelessness after rape. This makes the rage item clinically discordant within the selected five components.

issues.item: Constant Socialising: I keep myself constantly surrounded by people so I am never alone with my thoughts
issues.explanation: The strategy of constant socialising is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile in this rape-related presentation. The selected triggers are solitary/sensory reminders (silence, outdoor smells, anniversary), and the appraisals are shame, suicidality, and feared rage. Constantly surrounding oneself with people does not connect clearly to these reminders and is somewhat at odds with body shame after rape, making it the least coherent avoidance/coping item here.

vignette: Clara was twenty-nine when the assault occurred on a stretch of fallow land behind her family's plot. The air had gone completely still, the kind of silence that swallows sound whole, and the turned earth beneath her boots had released a thick, wet scent. When it was over, the calendar already bore a date she would come to dread every autumn. In the months that followed, the quiet weeks stretched into a long, unbroken tension. She found that certain smells, like freshly tilled soil or rain on dry leaves, would catch her in the throat. Silence, when it fell suddenly on the porch or between rows of crops, made her breath catch as if she were back in that exact pocket of stillness. Each year on that same date, the calendar seemed to press against her ribs, marking a boundary she could not cross without feeling the past rise up. She did not name what was happening; she simply adapted. She forced herself to speak only of bright things, telling herself that life still held good days, that she should be grateful for the sun and the harvest. She began avoiding places that held no light, stepping around the unlit toolshed, refusing to descend into the dark root cellar where the air hung heavy and still. She wore long sleeves even in the height of August and kept her hands tucked in her pockets, because she could not bear the thought of anyone laying a palm on her skin. She told herself to push through, to count the blessings of a stable partnership and a steady paycheck, but the positive thoughts felt distant and thin. Her partner, Marcus, had tried to stay close, yet she had come to believe that proximity was a danger she must guard against, and they had adjusted their sleep and their routines around the quiet distance between them. Now at seventy-four, Clara still rises before dawn to walk her rows, though the work has grown heavier. She moves through the fields carefully, her boots scuffing the topsoil, and whenever the wind shifts and carries the rich, damp odor of the earth up to her, her shoulders lock and her mind fractures into that old stillness. What frightened her most was the slow erosion of her own worth; she was not sure her life was worth living anymore, that she had nothing left to hold onto. When she looked at her hands or caught her reflection in the kitchen window, she felt ashamed of what happened to her body, convinced it was now a vessel that had been violated rather than her own. She scrubbed her skin until it reddened, certain that she felt dirty or contaminated because of what happened, a residue that clung beneath the surface no matter how long she stood under the water. It was this accumulation, the way the sudden silence in her own kitchen had begun to feel as heavy as the fields, that finally brought her to the clinic. She hopes to find a way to walk the soil without her lungs catching, and perhaps, just perhaps, to stop carrying the weight of a past that refuses to stay buried.
